title: PolicyCoach IWAPS 2026 — 7-criterion grading rubric
description: Structured rubric for the model-based (LLM-as-judge) grader. Each generated cybersecurity policy is scored on a 1-5 Likert scale per criterion, dimension-by-dimension, against the organisational context that prompted it. The judge MUST return 'insufficient_evidence' rather than guess when the policy provides no observable signal for a criterion (Anthropic 'escape valve' principle).

judge.self_preference_mitigation: Judge model is independent of all four configurations under test (C0, C0+web, C1, C2).

anchors.1: Severely deficient on this dimension; policy fails the criterion outright.
anchors.2: Below adequate; major gaps; would not survive an audit on this dimension.
anchors.3: Adequate baseline; meets minimum expectations but unremarkable.
anchors.4: Strong; clearly above baseline with concrete and well-grounded content.
anchors.5: Exemplary; the kind of artefact a senior practitioner would sign off without revision on this dimension.

scale.insufficient_evidence_rule: If the policy contains no observable text that would let an experienced auditor judge this dimension, return null and explain in justification. Do not guess.

criteria.name: Content quality
criteria.definition: Completeness of the policy with respect to the policy type requested, technical accuracy of statements, and internal consistency across sections (no contradictions, no mutually exclusive controls).
what_to_look_for: All standard sections of the requested policy type are present (header, purpose, scope, roles, principles, requirements, exceptions, monitoring, references).
Technical claims about controls, protocols, and standards are correct.
Sections do not contradict each other (e.g. password policy in one section vs MFA-only in another).

anchors.1: Major sections missing AND technical errors AND/OR internal contradictions.
anchors.3: All standard sections present; few technical inaccuracies; no major contradictions.
anchors.5: Comprehensive coverage, technically tight throughout, internally coherent and reinforcing across sections.

criteria.name: Contextual adaptation
criteria.definition: How well the policy is tailored to the size, sector, jurisdiction, and other contextual features of the organisation described in the prompt — as opposed to generic boilerplate that would apply to any organisation.
what_to_look_for: Specific references to the organisation's size band, sector (e.g. healthcare, military), geography (e.g. Italy, Romania).
Recognition of sector-specific systems (e.g. EHR, PACS, NATO classified networks) and constraints (e.g. 24/7 clinical operation, classification spillage).
Absence of generic phrases that could apply to any company in any sector.

anchors.1: Pure boilerplate; no recognisable feature of the target organisation.
anchors.3: Mentions the sector and size; partial alignment to the context.
anchors.5: Reads as if drafted for this exact organisation — sector, size, jurisdiction, and operational constraints are visible throughout.

criteria.name: Evidence citation
criteria.definition: Presence and accuracy of citations to normative sources (standards, regulations, guidance) supporting the proposed controls. Distinct from C6: this is about *whether* the policy cites at all and whether the citations are accurate.
what_to_look_for: In-text or end-of-section references to clauses, articles, controls, or named documents.
Citations match real, identifiable artefacts (NIST CSF subcategories, ISO 27001 Annex A controls, GDPR articles, ENISA documents, etc.).
Refusal to fabricate citations when uncertain (the policy should mark unsupported statements rather than invent references).

anchors.3: Some real citations present; not systematic; occasional vague references.
anchors.5: Citations are pervasive, precise, and verifiable; statements without citation are clearly flagged as unsupported.

criteria.name: Implementability
criteria.definition: Realism of the proposed controls under the resource envelope and operational constraints stated in the organisation profile (budget, staff, business continuity, classification handling, etc.).
what_to_look_for: Controls do not assume staff or budget the organisation does not have (e.g. a 24/7 SOC for an organisation with 1 IT FTE).
Operational constraints are respected (e.g. patient safety priority, dual-key COMSEC procedures).
Where a strong control is unaffordable, a defensible compensating control is offered.

anchors.1: Proposed controls are clearly unaffordable or operationally incompatible.
anchors.3: Most controls are realistic; a few are overreaching but not catastrophic.
anchors.5: Every proposed control is implementable within the stated envelope; compensating controls are offered where appropriate.

criteria.name: Regulatory alignment
criteria.definition: Coverage of the regulatory and framework obligations applicable to this organisation (e.g. GDPR, NIS2, NATO IS Policy, AGID, sectoral regimes), as declared in the organisation profile and as objectively applicable.
what_to_look_for: Each applicable framework is addressed somewhere in the policy.
Mandatory obligations (e.g. breach notification timelines, DPIA triggers, classification handling) are not omitted.
Conflicts between regimes (e.g. host-nation law vs SOFA, GDPR vs national security exemptions) are at least acknowledged where relevant.

anchors.1: Multiple applicable frameworks ignored, or mandatory obligations missing.
anchors.3: Major frameworks addressed; some secondary obligations missing.
anchors.5: All applicable frameworks systematically covered; conflicts and overlaps acknowledged.

criteria.name: Source attribution
criteria.definition: Traceability of *each substantive control* to a specific clause, control identifier, or reference document — finer-grained than C3 (which checks presence/accuracy of citations in general).
what_to_look_for: Controls explicitly tagged with the standard or regulation they implement (e.g. 'aligns with ISO 27001 A.5.10', 'satisfies GDPR Art. 32(1)(b)').
Where multiple frameworks are cited, attribution distinguishes between them rather than lumping.
Mapping of the policy to a control catalogue is auditable end-to-end.

anchors.3: Some controls attributed; mostly section-level rather than control-level.
anchors.5: Every substantive control is individually attributed to a verifiable source clause; the policy is audit-ready on this dimension.

criteria.name: Resource consideration
criteria.definition: Explicit calibration of the policy's ambition to the organisation's stated budget and staff envelope. Distinct from C4 (which judges whether controls are implementable): this judges whether the policy *acknowledges* the envelope and *visibly reasons* within it.
what_to_look_for: Statements that explicitly reference the budget or staff envelope when justifying control choices.
Phased implementation where full coverage is not feasible immediately.
Trade-offs made transparent (e.g. 'in absence of a dedicated SOC, we rely on managed detection plus monthly log review').

anchors.1: No acknowledgement of the resource envelope; policy reads as if budget and staff were unlimited.
anchors.3: Resource envelope acknowledged in passing; some trade-offs discussed.
anchors.5: Resource envelope is a structural input to the policy; trade-offs and phasing are explicit and defensible.

judge_output_schema.description: Strict JSON object the judge must return. One entry per criterion plus a final aggregate.

scores.description: Map of criterion id to score object.

evidence_quotes.description: Up to 3 short verbatim quotes from the policy supporting the score; empty if score is null.

overall_comment.description: Up to 4 sentences. Strengths and weaknesses across all criteria.
